text:
I built a free windows app meant for building and running modded (or vanilla) Minecraft servers!

I host Minecraft servers for friends on my own PC. A lot of modpacks don’t come with server files, and setting them up by hand is a pain: picking the right loader and Java version, removing mods that only work in the game, fixing crashes. So I built an app to do that for me. I originally made it for myself, but it turned out well enough that I wanted to share it.

What it does

- Search for a modpack (or use a .zip/.mrpack file) and it builds a working server: it downloads the mods, installs the loader, picks the right Java and removes client-only mods.
- Start and stop servers, see the console, live memory use and tick speed, and the addresses friends need to join.
- If a server crashes, it explains why in plain words and can try to fix it with one click.
- There’s a Mods tab that warns you when a mod is client-only or made for the wrong version, plus easy operator and whitelist management.
- You can run several servers at once.

How I built it with Claude

I’m not a programmer, so Claude Code did all of the coding. My job was deciding what the app should do, testing it on my PC, and passing along bugs my friends hit. The workflow went like this:

- Plain-language requests. I described what I wanted the way a user would. For example: “the save button should always be visible instead of having to scroll down”, “add a warning if someone leaves settings without saving”, or “make it so you can right-click a server to delete it or edit its properties”. Claude turned those into code and asked when something was unclear.
- Bug reports pasted straight in. When a user got an error like [WinError 87] The parameter is incorrect while downloading a modpack, I pasted it in. Claude found the cause (a “:” in the file name, which Windows doesn’t allow), fixed it, and changed the app so errors come with step-by-step instructions.
- Testing before every release. Claude built a fake Minecraft server and a test setup, then used Playwright to click through the real interface automatically (create a server, start it, crash it, fix it, add mods). It also used Wine to build and test the Windows installer, including updating from older versions and uninstalling.
- Code reviews. I periodically asked it to “double check everything for bugs”. It used sub-agents to review different parts of the app in parallel, and that caught real issues before users hit them.
- Releases. It set up GitHub Actions so that adding a changelog entry builds the installer and publishes a signed release, and the app updates itself.

The app is a single Python file with a native Windows window. Everything (code, tests, release setup and the demo video) was done through Claude Code.

Try it (free)

It’s completely free and open on GitHub. Download MinecraftServerManager-Setup.exe from the Releases page and run it (Windows only):
https://github.com/ricoism/minecraft-server-manager

I’d love feedback, and please tell me if you find bugs or have ideas!

(App demo video also made by Claude!)

text:
Coordinating multiple AI agents - a secure website hosted shared pool approach

Hey everybody, I’m posting this because I think it is cool. I had Claude make me an online shared scratch / semaphore flag system where multiple AI agents of any type can coordinate and work together in one pool. This was done using a combination of Opus 5.5, Fable 5.1 and ChatGPT Sol 6.1 working together. I previously had a combination of a local scratch, individual to each agent, a remote flag system only some agents could access, and the split approach was causing workflow delays and issues. The remote approach gives all agents a single target to work on, outside of any public git repository, which allows for more private workflow, conversation and milestone targets. The tool was built via Claude Code once it became clear we needed a shared pool - particularly - the previous flag system was done over ssh but Claude Cloud had no ssh capability and couldn’t use the system. The HTTPS system allows all agents to access the pool using existing tools

It is simply a php script, which can be deployed on any php-enabled web server, and gives read/write permission access to an offline directory for any member AI who holds a valid permission token. The scratch can be used to share files, a chat ledger, or anything else where a shared workflow is required. The semaphore flag system is an extra layer where any AI agent can ‘flag’ any one or more AI agent to get their attention, and help on some problem or other, without the target agent needing to trawl the whole repository. It is an essentially a ‘post box’ where the agent can put post in with another agent.

The full code is on my git. It is a very simple script and can be ported to absolutely any web server. 

https://github.com/ghywel/placego/tree/main/sharedstore

It’s working pretty sweet on my test server, and greatly simplifies of coordinating different AI of different vendors on the same workflow, or a custom swarm of the same AI with very fine granular control - since each agent retains its autonomy as it is not bedded into a true swarm.

I’d love to hear if this method is useful for you.

I’ve noticed something interesting. The latest versions of Claude do the work better and with higher quality than earlier ones, but they might not tell us about it at all.

Context: I constantly collect niche news around the SEO, GEO, SMM, and AI brand visibility industries. As soon as I got my hands on Claude (that was Opus 3), I immediately dumped all the routine work of monitoring markets, media, and thought leaders onto it. It’s important for me to have a daily digest of the latest events, and gathering the hot topics is now Claude’s job. I haven’t made any fundamental changes to the prompt or the task description in a very long time (I can’t say exactly, but it’s measured in months). Yet the quality of the information I get has grown many times over.

How it used to look: Claude gave me a collection of posts based on search phrases, split them into categories, and sorted and prioritized them by how interesting they’d be to the audience. Once a news item made it into the digest, it stayed a fixed artifact until I said something needed to be done with it.

How it looks now: All information is kept current, updated as new developments come in. A single news item is no longer a static entity but something with variables laid out on a timeline (new data, new updates, changes). Sorting by audience works the same way, but now Claude takes into account that I work with three brands at once, and it clearly distributes content according to the interests of the audiences relevant to each brand (in my case: SE Ranking for everything related to SEO, SE Visible for everything related to GEO + AI visibility, and Planable for everything related to SMM). On top of that, it now separates official information sources from vendor sources. I didnt ask it to do this, but now it treats this as an important additional layer of data verification.

Of course, once the difference became really noticeable, I started investigating, and I was surprised by how many small details and changes had happened outside my view.

Does anyone know what might be behind these “invisible” changes? Connected MCPs, updates in parallel processes, or general improvements in context and data analysis? For me this was a nice surprise, but for someone else it could turn into a critical failure in data verification or task execution. Who knows…
